scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and the answer depends on several factors, including the context of your relationship, the child’s well-being, and the legal framework in place. Based on your description, I’d give this scenario a **0** (not an asshole, but there are valid concerns and potential pitfalls to consider). Here’s why: ### **Why it’s not inherently wrong (0):** 1. **Boundaries are necessary** – You’ve been accommodating for years, and it’s understandable that you’re now asserting your rights. Continuously bending to your ex’s demands—especially when they disrupt your legally agreed-upon time—can lead to resentment and further imbalance. 2. **Your son’s best interest** – If you feel that your ex is consistently prioritizing her own convenience over your parenting time (e.g., canceling visits last-minute, rescheduling without notice), it’s reasonable to push back. Children thrive on stability, and they should not be used as pawns in adult conflicts. 3. **Legal enforcement** – If the court has already set a schedule, you’re within your rights to insist on it. If she’s repeatedly violating it, you may need to escalate this legally (e.g., through mediation or court enforcement). 4. **Your son’s perspective** – At 8 years old, your son is old enough to understand routines. If he’s being shuffled around without warning, it could create instability. Keeping him during her family event (if it’s truly disrupting your schedule) might actually be a way to protect his consistency. ### **Potential concerns (why it’s not a perfect solution):** - **Escalation risk** – If you keep your son without legal justification, your ex may retaliate (e.g., by refusing future visits or involving authorities). This could harm your relationship with her and, indirectly, your son’s relationship with her. - **Child’s feelings** – If your son is close to his mother’s family, abruptly keeping him could cause confusion or guilt. He might feel torn between you and her. - **Long-term damage** – If this becomes a pattern, it could turn into a custody battle, which is stressful for everyone, especially the child. ### **What you could do instead:** 1. **Document everything** – Keep records of all missed visits, last-minute changes, and communications. This strengthens your case if you need to go to court. 2. **Negotiate a fair schedule** – Propose a compromise, such as: - Swapping weekends *only* when both of you agree in advance (not last-minute). - Ensuring your son’s activities don’t fall on your parenting time unless you both agree. - Setting clear rules (e.g., "No more than one rescheduling per month"). 3. **Legal recourse** – If she continues to violate the court order, consult a family lawyer to enforce the agreement. Some courts have "contempt of court" provisions for repeated violations. 4. **Focus on co-parenting** – Even if you’re frustrated, try to keep the child out of the conflict. Frame your requests as "for the sake of our son’s routine" rather than "because I’m tired of being taken advantage of." ### **Final Thought:** You’re not the asshole for standing up for your rights, but you *are* the asshole if you do so in a way that harms your son’s relationship with his mother or creates more chaos. **The goal should be fairness, not revenge.** If you can’t reach a mutual agreement, legal action may be necessary—but try mediation first.
